claims.text: A hybrid workflow can couple sparse, short ab initio molecular-dynamics data with a machine-learning interatomic potential trained for solid and liquid states near fusion.
The hybrid workflow can substantially reduce the computational cost of obtaining free energies for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
An ML potential trained on both phases will faithfully retain vibrational-entropy contributions.
An ML potential trained on both phases will faithfully retain anharmonic effects.
An ML potential trained on both phases will faithfully retain electron–vibration coupling effects.
Limited ab initio MD at selected temperatures can provide reference data sufficient to interpolate the free-energy surface over the entire high-temperature regime.
A machine-learning potential calibrated on solid and liquid configurations can accurately sample their free-energy landscapes.
Sparse ab initio calibration points enable accelerated exploration of the free-energy landscape.
Machine-learning models can attain near-DFT accuracy in elemental and multicomponent materials while offering a favorable balance between accuracy and computational cost.
The hybrid method will predict solid–liquid phase free energies with fidelity similar to explicit ab initio MD or TOR-TILD.
The hybrid method will predict melting temperatures with fidelity similar to explicit ab initio MD or TOR-TILD.
The hybrid method will be at least approximately ten times faster than explicit ab initio MD or TOR-TILD.
Hybrid-method predictions should agree within acceptable error margins with benchmarks from simpler elemental or binary systems.
The method is expected to apply near fusion to high-entropy alloys containing up to five principal elements.
Earlier simpler-system studies suggest significant speedups with retained fidelity.
The exact speedup and error margins in complex high-entropy alloys remain uncertain until systematic benchmarking is performed.
